I don't know how it is now, but I do know that in many trials historically, they give one of the patient groups a placebo or a medication with "well known" properties - which in at least one case that I can recall, means giving them crap that they know doesn't work. When this is done, it will lead to a cancer patient becoming the corpse of a cancer patient.

This is done for the purposes of statistical purity. While there are advantages to this method, the simple fact of the matter is that you're playing Russian Roulette with a loaded weapon here so that someone can publish their results. If I have a choice between a medication that could be better but has at least a somewhat decent chance of saving my life, versus being administered snake oil so some researcher can set the "deceased" variable in their spreadsheet to "yes" and run an ANOVA on it, the researcher should not be surprised that people aren't willing to die for him.

As I said, I don't know how this is now. Hopefully nowadays they give the control group the standard treatment and compare the new therapy against that.
